div.p: Your AI coding assistant — Claude, Cursor, Copilot, or a local model — doesn't know what TVBO is until you tell it. We ship a bundle of focused skills that teaches your assistant about the three pillars, the model spec format, backend choices, and this platform. Install once, then every session benefits.
Large language models are powerful but oblivious. Without context they hallucinate parameter names, pick the wrong backend, or hand-edit generated code. The skills carry the rules they need.
The same canonical skill renders as a Claude Code skill, a Copilot instruction, a Cursor rule, or a raw system prompt. Pick the target that fits your workflow — no copy-paste between formats.
Skills evolve as TVBO evolves. Re-running tvbo skills install after an upgrade keeps your assistant aligned with the current API, schema, and backend support.
The skills work for every level. Here's where to start.
Let the AI assistant teach you. Install the skills, then ask "What is TVBO and how do I write my first model?" — you'll get a guided walkthrough with copy-pasteable code.
Best target: claude-code or cursor.
You know the YAML format and have a backend preference. The skills stop your assistant from making rookie mistakes (label vs name, value on a state variable, wrong extras for a backend).
Best target: claude-code + agents-md for your project repo.

Six maintainer skills ship in the TVBO repository itself — covering git policy, surgical coding discipline, LinkML schema regen, codegen templates, the pytest marker matrix, and the design-review workflow.
Best target: repo-local — they're already in .claude/skills/ when you clone.

pre.code:
# Default: Claude Code, user scope tvbo skills install
# Or Cursor: tvbo skills install --target cursor
# Or a system prompt for raw API / local model: tvbo skills install --target prompt > tvbo-system.md

# Show what would be installed tvbo skills install --dry-run
# List installed skills ls ~/.claude/skills/tvbo-*
# Remove cleanly when you're done tvbo skills uninstall

div.p: TVBO marks every file it writes with a managed-by: tvbo frontmatter line. Upgrades overwrite our own files safely; files you've customised are left alone unless you pass --force.
Four user skills land on your machine. Each fires on demand when the conversation matches its topic — they cost nothing when you're working on something else.

How to specify a Dynamics in YAML or Python. Catches the common errors: putting value on a state variable, mixing LaTeX and Python syntax, name mismatches in the equation RHS.

div.h2: Ready to ship your first agent-assisted TVBO model?
div.p: Once your assistant knows TVBO, it can scaffold a Dynamics, pick the right backend, run a simulation, plot the result, and even push the experiment to this platform — all in a single conversation.

div.h1: An executable knowledge framework for brain-network modelling
div.p: TVB-O represents a whole-brain model and the experiment that runs it as one typed, ontology-grounded specification. One compiler generates runnable code and a methods report from it, and an ontology across four domains makes models comparable across the literature.

div.h2: No shared representation of what a model is

div.p: A published brain model is usually bespoke code. It can drift from the equations in the paper, is often shared with missing parameters, and stays hard to run because results depend on software versions and execution environments, so results are difficult to reproduce and compare.

Underneath lies a single absence: no shared, machine-readable representation of what a model is, or of the whole simulation experiment around it, with its network, inputs, execution and analyses. TVB-O supplies that representation, following the example set by SBML and BioModels in systems biology.

div.h2: Four pillars: specify, compile, ground, open
div.p: A simulation experiment is written down once as a specification. It compiles to code and a methods report, it is grounded in a knowledge graph, and both are open to people and to coding agents.

svg.aria-label: One typed SimulationExperiment compiles to code and a methods report and is grounded in a knowledge graph; the platform and the Python package open both to people and coding agents.
svg.text: Runnable code and a methods report
Knowledge Graph, Experiment Builder, REST API and the tvbo Python package, for people and coding agents

div.p: A LinkML schema types the whole simulation experiment. The Python classes are generated from it, so the specification and the code stay in step.
One compiler turns a specification into runnable code for each backend and into a methods report, so the paper and the code come from the same source.

An ontology generated from the same schema links entities to terms for physical units, biological processes, brain anatomy and clinical disorders, so models written in different notation can be compared.
The tvbo Python package, the curated knowledge base and this platform: browse, build and share experiments in the browser or from Python.
Not only the model: the network it runs on, how it is integrated, what is observed, how it is explored and analysed, and the software it runs with. Each part is checked against the schema.

SBML executes and grounds biochemical models, NeuroML does both for cells and spiking networks, and PyRates compiles whole-brain models to several backends. TVB-O builds on these and brings specification, execution and grounding together for whole-brain models and the experiments around them.

div.h2: Built with The Virtual Brain, not instead of it

div.p: TVB-O is not a fork of The Virtual Brain. It is a specification and knowledge layer that treats TVB as one of several backends. The same types describe any dynamical system on any network, from a single Lorenz attractor to a lattice of oscillators or a power grid, so the framework reaches beyond whole-brain simulation while staying native to it.
It aligns to and extends EBRAINS resources such as openMINDS and the Model Catalog, and works alongside NeuroML/LEMS, BIDS and SBML.

div.h2: Developed at Charité and the BIH
div.p: TVB-O is developed in the Brain Simulation Section at Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin and the Berlin Institute of Health (BIH), the group behind The Virtual Brain.
